title: Interpret PLSpredict and avoid train/test leakage

brief.text: SEM Studio does not compute PLSpredict or CVPAT yet. This is a concept challenge: the output below is illustrative, as a dedicated R package would report it for a TAM model (10 folds, 10 repetitions); it was not computed by SEM Studio.
brief.title: Concept challenge

brief.text: A team reports R²(BI) = .33 and writes "the model has high predictive power". Their PLSpredict output for the three BI indicators (prediction errors on held-out folds):

items: bi1: Q²predict = .14; RMSE PLS = 1.21, RMSE LM = 1.24
bi2: Q²predict = .12; RMSE PLS = 1.30, RMSE LM = 1.28
bi3: Q²predict = .11; RMSE PLS = 1.25, RMSE LM = 1.27

brief.text: Before running PLSpredict, the team had dropped two BI items with low loadings in the full sample and tried three model variants, keeping the one with the best PLSpredict result.

tasks.prompt: Does R²(BI) = .33 support the claim of "high predictive power"?

options.text: No. R² is in-sample explanatory power; predictive power has to be shown out of sample against a benchmark.
Yes, R² above .25 means the model predicts well.
options.feedback: R² thresholds describe in-sample explanation and say nothing about new cases.

options.text: Yes, because the paths are significant.
options.feedback: Significance concerns parameters, not prediction of new observations.

tasks.prompt: What do the positive Q²predict values show?

options.text: The model's out-of-sample predictions beat the naive training-mean prediction for every BI indicator.
options.feedback: Correct. Q²predict > 0 compares with the mean benchmark only.

options.text: The model predicts better than the linear-model benchmark.
options.feedback: That comparison uses RMSE (or MAE) against LM, not Q²predict.

options.text: The model explains 11–14% of the variance of BI.
options.feedback: Q²predict is a relative prediction-error measure, not an explained-variance share.

tasks.prompt: Compare RMSE of PLS with the LM benchmark. Following Shmueli et al. (2019), what predictive power does this suggest?

options.text: Medium: PLS has lower prediction error than LM for the majority (two of three) of the indicators.
options.feedback: Correct. All lower = high, majority = medium, minority = low, none = no predictive power (in their guidelines).

options.text: High: PLS beats LM for all indicators.
options.feedback: For bi2, PLS (1.30) is worse than LM (1.28).
Q²predict is not compared with R² thresholds; the LM comparison decides the level.

tasks.prompt: Which steps leaked information from the evaluation data into model building? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dropping BI items based on full-sample loadings before cross-validation.
options.feedback: Correct. The held-out folds influenced the measurement model.

options.text: Choosing among three model variants by their PLSpredict results and reporting only the best.
options.feedback: Correct. The cross-validation became part of model selection; its result is optimistic.
Repetitions stabilise the estimate; they do not leak information.

options.text: Comparing PLS with an LM benchmark.
options.feedback: Benchmarks are part of a proper assessment.

hints: What data were used to compute R², and what data are used to compute Q²predict?
Q²predict and the LM comparison use different benchmarks; check which one each statement refers to.
Ask of every step: did the cases that later served as test folds influence this decision?

solution.text: R² = .33 is in-sample explanation. The positive Q²predict values show that the model beats the naive mean out of sample; PLS beats the LM benchmark for two of three indicators, which Shmueli et al. (2019) would call medium predictive power. However, dropping items on full-sample results and selecting the best of three variants by PLSpredict leak information, so even these results are optimistic. A clean assessment fixes the model in advance (or selects it inside the training folds only) and runs the cross-validation once.
